Dissection describes three parts: a genu, a stem and a fan.
Bilateral subcortical lesions are reported to cause cortical deafness or auditory agnosia.

quiz.q: Which compact tract carries auditory information from the medial geniculate nucleus to Heschl's gyrus?
Bilateral subcortical lesions leave vision intact but cause cortical deafness. Which pathway is interrupted?

how_we_know: The bundle is small and hard to image, so the evidence comes from histological atlases, fibre dissection in postmortem brains, and tractography in volunteers, and from rare patients with bilateral lesions. Stimulation data for the bundle itself do not exist in the studies found here.

evidence.claim: Dissection and tractography show a transverse bundle from thalamus to posterior temporal lobe
evidence.finding: Maffei and colleagues combined micro-dissection of three human hemispheres with tractography from four Human Connectome Project datasets. Both approaches showed a transverse course from the midline to the posterior temporal lobe, and dissection showed a genu, stem and fan.
evidence.quote: The acoustic radiation is a compact bundle of fibers conveying auditory information from the medial geniculate nucleus of the thalamus to the auditory cortex. Both techniques show the unique trajectory of the AR, a transversal course from the midline to the lateral convexity of the posterior temporal lobe.
evidence.cite: Maffei C, Jovicich J, De Benedictis A, et al. Topography of the human acoustic radiation as revealed by ex vivo fibers micro-dissection and in vivo diffusion-based tractography. Brain Struct Funct. 2018;223(1):449-459.

evidence.claim: Bilateral white matter lesions that overlap the radiation cause cortical deafness with vision spared
evidence.finding: Poliva and colleagues used probabilistic tractography in 19 healthy adults, then overlaid the lesions from eight published patients with severe auditory agnosia or cortical deafness. In all eight, bilateral lesions overlapped one or both components of a proposed dorsal branch of the acoustic radiation while visual fields were preserved. The authors say the course of the radiation is not settled.
evidence.quote: In all eight historical cases, bilateral lesions overlapped one or both components of the dAR while visual fields were preserved, suggesting relative sparing of the optic radiations and the vAR.
evidence.cite: Poliva O, Liu Y, Rafal RD. Auditory radiations: Evidence for dorsal and ventral branches. Hear Res. 2026;472:109551.

evidence.claim: The radiation is included in a stereotaxic atlas built from ten postmortem brains
evidence.finding: Burgel and colleagues mapped fibre tracts in myelin-stained sections of ten postmortem brains and registered them to a standard space. The atlas includes the acoustic radiation, together with the medial geniculate nucleus as its source.
evidence.quote: The analyzed tracts include the corticospinal tract, optic and acoustic radiations, fornix, cingulum, corpus callosum, superior longitudinal, superior and inferior occipito-frontal and uncinate fascicles; sources and targets of fiber tracts include the lateral and medial geniculate nuclei and mamillary bodies.
evidence.cite: Burgel U, Amunts K, Hoemke L, Mohlberg H, Gilsbach JM, Zilles K. White matter fiber tracts of the human brain: three-dimensional mapping at microscopic resolution, topography and intersubject variability. Neuroimage. 2006;29(4):1092-105.

hint: limbic white matter arch curving over the callosal body
summary: The cingulum is a long association bundle that lies within the cingulate gyrus and curves around the corpus callosum from the front of the brain to the medial temporal lobe. It contains fibres of many lengths, from short links between neighbouring cingulate areas to long connections between the frontal lobe and the parahippocampal gyrus. It links the anterior and posterior cingulate cortex, the medial prefrontal cortex, the precuneus and the medial temporal lobe. It is a major white matter route of the limbic system and of the default mode network. Lesions of the cingulum are used to treat intractable obsessive-compulsive disorder and pain.
where: On a medial view the cingulum runs as a belt just beneath the cingulate gyrus and above the corpus callosum. It starts near the subcallosal area, arches over the genu, body and splenium, and descends into the parahippocampal gyrus. The model shows the dense core of the bundle from a probabilistic histology atlas, not every short fibre. A medial or sagittal view shows it best.
does: It carries communication among medial frontal, cingulate, parietal and medial temporal regions that deal with emotion, memory, attention and evaluation. Catani and colleagues used tractography to show it in living people, among nine other fasciculi, and found the virtual maps matched the classical postmortem descriptions. The bundle contains many short fibres, so tractography of its whole length does not mean single axons run from front to back. Its function is inferred from imaging and lesion data and is not as well defined as that of the motor or visual tracts.
connects: It links the anterior cingulate and medial prefrontal cortex with the posterior cingulate and precuneus, and its lower part links them with the parahippocampal gyrus and entorhinal cortex. It is part of the Papez circuit and of the wiring of the default mode network.
clinical: In anterior cingulotomy for treatment-refractory obsessive-compulsive disorder, a lesion in the cingulate region improved symptoms in 32% to 45% of patients in one long-term series. Changes in cingulum integrity have been reported in Alzheimer's disease and other conditions, but a study in two cohorts of people with mild cognitive impairment found no link between cingulum integrity and amyloid or medial temporal atrophy.
remember: Cingulum means belt: it is the belt of white matter inside the cingulate gyrus, wrapped over the callosum.
facts: It runs within the cingulate gyrus above the corpus callosum.
In a 44-patient cingulotomy series for obsessive-compulsive disorder, 45% were at least partial responders.
Tractography reproduces the classical postmortem description of the cingulum.

quiz.q: Which association bundle lies within the cingulate gyrus and arches over the corpus callosum to the parahippocampal gyrus?
Anterior cingulotomy for refractory obsessive-compulsive disorder lesions which white matter bundle and cortex?
Which tract links the posterior cingulate with the entorhinal region and belongs to the Papez circuit?

how_we_know: Tractography shows the bundle in living people and agrees with postmortem descriptions. Evidence about function comes mainly from cingulotomy outcomes, which also remove cingulate cortex, and from correlations between integrity and disease. No study found here stimulates the bundle on its own.

evidence.claim: Tractography shows the cingulum and nine other fasciculi in living people
evidence.finding: Catani and colleagues used diffusion tensor tractography to display ten white matter structures, including the cingulum, in living people. The virtual maps were faithful to the classical postmortem descriptions of white matter anatomy.
evidence.quote: Specifically, we applied this technique to visualize in vivo (i) the superior longitudinal (arcuate) fasciculus, (ii) the inferior longitudinal fasciculus, (iii) the superior fronto-occipital (subcallosal) fasciculus, (iv) the inferior frontooccipital fasciculus, (v) the uncinate fasciculus, (vi) the cingulum, (vii) the anterior commissure, (viii) the corpus callosum, (ix) the internal capsule, and (x) the fornix.
evidence.cite: Catani M, Howard RJ, Pajevic S, Jones DK. Virtual in vivo interactive dissection of white matter fasciculi in the human brain. Neuroimage. 2002;17(1):77-94.

evidence.claim: Cingulotomy helps some patients with treatment-refractory obsessive-compulsive disorder
evidence.finding: Dougherty and colleagues followed 44 patients for a mean of 32 months after one or more cingulotomies. Fourteen patients (32%) met response criteria and six others (14%) were partial responders, so 20 patients (45%) were at least partial responders. This is causal evidence from an open series, without a control group.
evidence.quote: At mean follow-up of 32 months after one or more cingulotomies, 14 patients (32%) met criteria for treatment response and six others (14%) were partial responders. Thus, 20 patients (45%) were at least partial responders at long-term follow-up after one or more cingulotomies.
evidence.cite: Dougherty DD, Baer L, Cosgrove GR, et al. Prospective long-term follow-up of 44 patients who received cingulotomy for treatment-refractory obsessive-compulsive disorder. Am J Psychiatry. 2002;159(2):269-75.

evidence.claim: Cingulum integrity did not link amyloid to medial temporal atrophy in mild cognitive impairment
evidence.finding: Vlegels and colleagues tested whether the cingulum connects amyloid in the cingulate cortex with medial temporal atrophy in 21 memory clinic patients and 37 patients from a replication cohort. Cingulum integrity was not associated with either measure in either sample. This is a negative result that does not support the hypothesis.
evidence.quote: These findings, consistent in two independent cohorts, do not support our hypothesis that loss of white matter integrity of the cingulum is a connecting factor between cingulate gyrus Aβ deposition and MTL atrophy.
evidence.cite: Vlegels N, Ossenkoppele R, van der Flier WM, et al. Does Loss of Integrity of the Cingulum Bundle Link Amyloid-β Accumulation and Neurodegeneration in Alzheimer's Disease? J Alzheimers Dis. 2022;89(1):39-49.

hint: long bundle linking frontal and parietal lobes above the insula
summary: The superior longitudinal fasciculus is a large association bundle that links the frontal lobe with the parietal lobe and, in its arcuate part, with the temporal lobe. It runs above the insula and the putamen, lateral to the corona radiata. In humans it is described as three parts, SLF I to III, and the arcuate fasciculus curves around the sylvian fissure from the frontal to the temporal lobe. It carries information for spatial attention, in the right hemisphere especially, and for language, in the left. Damage causes neglect or aphasia depending on the side.
where: The model shows the dense core of the bundle from a probabilistic histology atlas. It lies in the deep white matter of the lateral hemisphere, above the insula and arching from the frontal operculum back toward the inferior parietal lobule. The arcuate part continues down into the temporal lobe. A lateral or axial view shows it best.
does: The fronto-parietal parts connect regions of the dorsal attention network and the frontoparietal control network. Catani and colleagues showed with tractography that the left arcuate fasciculus has a direct pathway between Broca and Wernicke territories and an indirect pathway through the inferior parietal cortex. In awake surgery, stimulating the arcuate fasciculus produces phonological errors, and stimulating the cortex where it ends can produce speech arrest. The bundle's role in the strict conduction aphasia model is debated, because cortical dysfunction alone can produce a similar picture.
connects: It links the superior and middle frontal gyri, the precentral gyrus and the inferior frontal gyrus with the superior and inferior parietal lobules, and the arcuate part links the frontal operculum with the posterior temporal lobe. It runs beside the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus and the uncinate fasciculus, which lie more ventrally.
clinical: Damage to the left arcuate fasciculus is linked to conduction aphasia, in which repetition is poor and phonemic paraphasias are frequent while comprehension is better preserved. Right-sided damage to the fronto-parietal connections is linked to spatial neglect. In semantic dementia the fronto-parietal SLF is relatively spared, whereas the arcuate and uncinate fasciculi are damaged.
remember: The superior longitudinal fasciculus is the long fronto-parietal highway above the insula, with the arcuate bend taking language to the temporal lobe.
facts: It has three parts in humans, SLF I, II and III, and the arcuate fasciculus curves toward the temporal lobe.
Stimulating the arcuate fasciculus in awake surgery produced phonological paraphasias in 6 of 13 patients.
It is relatively spared in semantic dementia.

quiz.q: Which large association bundle links frontal and parietal lobes above the insula, with an arcuate part toward the temporal lobe?
Poor repetition with fluent phonemic paraphasias and good comprehension classically follows damage to which bundle?
Which tract connects Broca's and Wernicke's territories directly and through an indirect route in the inferior parietal lobe?

how_we_know: Tractography maps the bundle in living people, and awake-surgery stimulation tests what happens when it is disturbed. Stroke and dementia studies give correlations with deficits. The classical conduction aphasia model has been questioned, because cortical stimulation alone can mimic it.

evidence.claim: Tractography shows a direct and an indirect pathway linking Broca and Wernicke territories
evidence.finding: Catani and colleagues averaged diffusion MRI from 11 right-handed healthy men and reconstructed the left arcuate fasciculus. Besides the classical direct pathway, they found an indirect pathway through the inferior parietal lobe, which helps explain the varied presentations of conduction aphasia. This is correlational evidence.
evidence.quote: Diffusion tensor magnetic resonance imaging data from 11 right-handed healthy male subjects were averaged, and the arcuate fasciculus of the left hemisphere reconstructed from this data using an interactive dissection technique. Beyond the classical arcuate pathway connecting Broca's and Wernicke's areas directly, we show a previously undescribed, indirect pathway passing through inferior parietal cortex.
evidence.cite: Catani M, Jones DK, ffytche DH. Perisylvian language networks of the human brain. Ann Neurol. 2005;57(1):8-16.

evidence.claim: Cortical stimulation alone can produce a conduction aphasia picture
evidence.finding: Anderson and colleagues stimulated the posterior superior temporal gyrus in an epilepsy patient. She made frequent phonemic paraphasias and repeated words poorly while her semantic knowledge was intact. This suggests that cortical dysfunction alone can cause conduction aphasia, and the arcuate fasciculus is not the only route to it. This is causal evidence in one patient.
evidence.quote: We observed an epileptic patient who, during cortical stimulation of her posterior superior temporal gyrus, demonstrated frequent phonemic paraphasias, decreased repetition of words, and yet had intact semantic knowledge, a pattern consistent with conduction aphasia. These findings suggest that cortical dysfunction alone may induce conduction aphasia.
evidence.cite: Anderson JM, Gilmore R, Roper S, et al. Conduction aphasia and the arcuate fasciculus: A reexamination of the Wernicke-Geschwind model. Brain Lang. 1999;70(1):1-12.

evidence.claim: Stimulating the arcuate fasciculus in awake surgery causes phonological errors
evidence.finding: Duffau and colleagues stimulated the white matter in 13 patients operated awake for glioma. Stimulating the inferior occipito-temporal fasciculus caused semantic paraphasias in all 13, and stimulating the arcuate fasciculus caused phonological paraphasias in 6. This is causal evidence.
evidence.quote: Subcortically, semantic paraphasia were induced in the 13 patients by stimulating the IOF, and phonological paraphasia were generated in 6 patients by stimulating the arcuate fasciculus.
evidence.cite: Duffau H, Gatignol P, Moritz-Gasser S, Mandonnet E. Is the left uncinate fasciculus essential for language? A cerebral stimulation study. J Neurol. 2009;256(3):382-9.

data.title: Patients with errors during white matter stimulation

evidence.claim: The fronto-parietal SLF is relatively spared in semantic dementia while arcuate and uncinate fibres are damaged
evidence.finding: Agosta and colleagues tracked language pathways in five patients with semantic dementia and eight healthy controls. The arcuate and uncinate fasciculi had significantly lower fractional anisotropy, whereas the fronto-parietal SLF was relatively spared. This is correlational evidence in a small sample.
evidence.quote: The arcuate and uncinate fasciculi demonstrated significantly higher mean diffusivity, parallel and transverse and significantly lower fractional anisotropy. The fronto-parietal superior longitudinal fasciculus was relatively spared, with a significant difference observed for transverse diffusivity and fractional anisotropy, only.
evidence.cite: Agosta F, Henry RG, Migliaccio R, et al. Language networks in semantic dementia. Brain. 2010;133(Pt 1):286-99.

stimulation.method: direct subcortical electrical stimulation during awake surgery
stimulation.effect: Stimulating the left arcuate fasciculus caused phonological paraphasias, which are sound-based word errors, in 6 of 13 patients.
stimulation.quote: Subcortically, semantic paraphasia were induced in the 13 patients by stimulating the IOF, and phonological paraphasia were generated in 6 patients by stimulating the arcuate fasciculus.
stimulation.cite: Duffau H, Gatignol P, Moritz-Gasser S, Mandonnet E. Is the left uncinate fasciculus essential for language? A cerebral stimulation study. J Neurol. 2009;256(3):382-9.

hint: ventral long bundle running through the extreme capsule
summary: The inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus is a long association bundle that runs along the ventral side of the hemisphere between the occipital and temporal regions and the frontal lobe. It passes through the extreme capsule, between the claustrum and the insular cortex. It is thought to carry the ventral semantic route of language and also non-verbal semantic information. Evidence for it comes from dissection and stimulation in awake surgery as well as tractography.
where: The model shows the dense core of the bundle from a probabilistic histology atlas. It runs from the occipital lobe forward through the temporal stem and the extreme capsule to the orbitofrontal and lateral frontal cortex. It lies below the arcuate and superior longitudinal fasciculi. An axial or lateral view shows it best.
does: Duffau and colleagues stimulated the white matter in 17 patients during awake surgery and located a main ventral subcortical pathway for semantics, within the dominant hemisphere, joining posterior and superior temporal areas with orbitofrontal and dorsolateral prefrontal regions. They proposed that it partly corresponds to this fasciculus. Herbet and colleagues later found that stimulation of the right-hemisphere fasciculus disturbed a non-verbal semantic task. It also carries visual information to the frontal lobe, though that part of its role is less established.
connects: It links the occipital and posterior temporal cortex with the orbitofrontal and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. It runs through the extreme capsule near the uncinate fasciculus, which joins the anterior temporal lobe to the orbitofrontal cortex through a hook.
clinical: Stimulating the left bundle during glioma surgery causes semantic paraphasias, so surgeons map and spare it. Right-sided stimulation can interrupt non-verbal semantic processing, such as matching pictures by meaning. The bundle is not a standard stroke localisation sign in the way the corticospinal tract is.
remember: The ventral highway: the occipital lobe and the frontal lobe joined through the extreme capsule, carrying meaning.
facts: It passes through the extreme capsule.
Stimulating it in awake surgery causes semantic paraphasias.
In 12 of 13 patients with a right-sided glioma, stimulation of the right bundle disturbed a non-verbal semantic task.

quiz.q: Which ventral association bundle passes through the extreme capsule and is stimulated to produce semantic paraphasias in awake surgery?
Which long tract joins occipital and temporal cortex to orbitofrontal cortex running beneath the arcuate fasciculus?

how_we_know: Awake surgery gives the strongest evidence: stimulation causes semantic errors at sites that match the course of the fasciculus. Postmortem fibre dissection and tractography agree on its course in humans. Some tracing studies in monkeys have questioned a direct occipital to frontal bundle, so its exact makeup is still discussed.

evidence.claim: Stimulating a ventral subcortical pathway causes semantic errors
evidence.finding: Duffau and colleagues operated on 17 patients with a low-grade glioma in the dominant hemisphere while they were awake. Stimulating cortical and subcortical sites caused semantic paraphasias. The authors concluded that there is a main ventral subcortical pathway for semantics that may partly correspond to the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus. This is causal evidence.
evidence.quote: Our results provide arguments in favour of the existence of a main ventral subcortical pathway underlying the semantic system, within the dominant hemisphere, joining the two essential cortical epicentres of this network: the posterior and superior temporal areas, and the orbitofrontal and dorsolateral prefontal regions. Such a ventral stream might anatomically partly correspond to the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus.
evidence.cite: Duffau H, Gatignol P, Mandonnet E, Peruzzi P, Tzourio-Mazoyer N, Capelle L. New insights into the anatomo-functional connectivity of the semantic system: a study using cortico-subcortical electrostimulations. Brain. 2005;128(Pt 4):797-810.

evidence.claim: The right-hemisphere bundle also supports non-verbal semantic processing
evidence.finding: Herbet and colleagues stimulated the right hemisphere in 13 patients awake for glioma. At the subcortical level they found non-verbal semantic sites in 12 patients, 15 sites in all, and every responsive point lay on the course of the right fasciculus. This is causal evidence.
evidence.quote: At the subcortical level, we found non-verbal semantic-related sites in all but one patient (n = 15 sites in 12 patients). Importantly, all these responsive stimulation points were located on the spatial course of the right inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus (IFOF).
evidence.cite: Herbet G, Moritz-Gasser S, Duffau H. Direct evidence for the contributive role of the right inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus in non-verbal semantic cognition. Brain Struct Funct. 2017;222(4):1597-1610.

stimulation.method: direct subcortical electrical stimulation during awake surgery
stimulation.effect: Stimulating the right-hemisphere bundle disrupted a picture-based non-verbal semantic task in 12 of 13 patients, and left-sided ventral stimulation caused semantic paraphasias.
stimulation.quote: At the subcortical level, we found non-verbal semantic-related sites in all but one patient (n = 15 sites in 12 patients). Importantly, all these responsive stimulation points were located on the spatial course of the right inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus (IFOF).
stimulation.cite: Herbet G, Moritz-Gasser S, Duffau H. Direct evidence for the contributive role of the right inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus in non-verbal semantic cognition. Brain Struct Funct. 2017;222(4):1597-1610.

hint: deep bundle beside the lateral ventricle, debated in humans
summary: The superior fronto-occipital fasciculus is a bundle that textbooks describe as running above the caudate nucleus and along the lateral ventricle from the frontal lobe back toward the parietal and occipital lobes. Whether it exists in the human brain is disputed. A connectome-based tractography and microdissection study concluded that it does not, and a second study found a bundle by tractography but not by dissection. The model shows what the histological atlas labels with this name, so treat the region as a contested structure and not an agreed tract. Its history of misidentified fibres is the main reason for the confusion.
where: The model shows the dense core of the bundle from a probabilistic histology atlas. It lies deep in the white matter above the caudate nucleus and just under the corpus callosum, running medial to the corona radiata along the lateral ventricle. Bao and colleagues found a bundle there by tractography that ended mainly in parietal cortex rather than the occipital lobe. A coronal or axial view shows the region best.
does: Its function is unsettled because its existence is. Thiebaut de Schotten and colleagues stimulated the white matter in awake patients and shifted line bisection to the right, and tracking identified the stimulated site as a section of the superior occipitofrontal fasciculus, a poorly known parietal-frontal pathway. Meola and colleagues later argued that reconstructions of this bundle come from false continuations between the superior thalamic peduncle and the stria terminalis. The fibres that stimulation disturbed may belong to a different bundle.
connects: In the classical description it links the frontal lobe with the parietal and occipital lobes above the lateral ventricle. Schmahmann and Pandya traced the history of the name, which began with a misidentification of aberrant callosal fibres in people without a corpus callosum.
clinical: No syndrome is reliably tied to this bundle, and the debate over its existence means that clinical claims should be treated with caution. The right-sided stimulation result suggests a role in symmetrical processing of the visual scene, but the fibres involved are disputed.
remember: Superior and inferior fronto-occipital fasciculi are a classic pair, but only the inferior one is well supported in humans.
facts: Meola and colleagues concluded in 2015 that the bundle does not exist in the human brain.
The term originated with Forel and Onufrowicz, who misidentified aberrant callosal fibres in patients with callosal agenesis.
Bao and colleagues found a tractography bundle that ends mainly in parietal cortex, not occipital cortex.

quiz.q: Which bundle, said to run above the caudate along the lateral ventricle, is argued not to exist in the human brain?
Which bundle's name began when Forel and Onufrowicz misidentified aberrant callosal fibres in callosal agenesis?

how_we_know: Be plain about this one: the evidence is in conflict. A study with deterministic tractography and microdissection concluded the bundle does not exist in humans, another study found it by tractography but not by dissection, and a stimulation study attributed an effect to it. Existence in monkeys is well documented.

evidence.claim: A connectome and dissection study concluded the bundle does not exist in humans
evidence.finding: Meola and colleagues applied deterministic tractography to a template of 488 healthy people and to 80 Human Connectome Project subjects, and checked the results by dissection of postmortem brains. They found that earlier reconstructions came from false continuations between known tracts, and no other fibre tract in that location.
evidence.quote: The imaging results showed that previous reconstructions of the SFOF were generated by two false continuations, namely between superior thalamic peduncle (STP) and stria terminalis (ST), and ST and posterior thalamic peduncle. The anatomical microdissection confirmed this finding. No other fiber tracts in the previously described location of the SFOF were identified. Hence, our data suggest that the SFOF does not exist in the human brain.
evidence.cite: Meola A, Comert A, Yeh FC, Stefaneanu L, Fernandez-Miranda JC. The controversial existence of the human superior fronto-occipital fasciculus: Connectome-based tractographic study with microdissection validation. Hum Brain Mapp. 2015;36(12):4964-71.

evidence.claim: Tractography finds a bundle there, but dissection does not confirm it
evidence.finding: Bao and colleagues ran diffusion spectrum imaging in six adults and in a template of 842 Human Connectome Project subjects, then dissected four postmortem brains. Tractography showed a compact fascicle above the caudate that ended mainly in parietal cortex. They could not identify it in dissection.
evidence.quote: We consider that this fiber bundle observed by tractography is the SFOF, although it terminates mainly at the parietal region, rather than occipital lobe. By contrast, we were unable to identify a fiber bundle corresponding to the SFOF in our fiber dissection study.
evidence.cite: Bao Y, Wang Y, Wang W, Wang Y. The Superior Fronto-Occipital Fasciculus in the Human Brain Revealed by Diffusion Spectrum Imaging Tractography: An Anatomical Reality or a Methodological Artifact? Front Neuroanat. 2017;11:119.

evidence.claim: The name came from a misidentification of callosal fibres
evidence.finding: Schmahmann and Pandya reviewed the history of the term. It started when Forel and Onufrowicz mistook aberrant longitudinal callosal fibres in patients with callosal agenesis for a fronto-occipital bundle, and Dejerine later described an actual fascicle that could not be told apart from the subcallosal fasciculus of Muratoff.
evidence.quote: The term "FOF" originated with Forel and Onufrowicz who misidentified aberrant longitudinally oriented callosal fibers in patients with callosal agenesis. This error was soon recognized, and Dejerine described an actual FOF linking frontal and occipital lobes, but gross dissection and lesion-degeneration methods could not distinguish the FOF from the subcallosal fasciculus of Muratoff and neighboring white matter bundles.
evidence.cite: Schmahmann JD, Pandya DN. The complex history of the fronto-occipital fasciculus. J Hist Neurosci. 2007;16(4):362-77.

stimulation.method: intraoperative electrical stimulation of the white matter during awake surgery
stimulation.effect: Stimulating the right inferior parietal lobule or deep white matter caused a rightward shift on a line bisection task, strongest with subcortical stimulation. The authors tracked the stimulated site as this bundle, but later work disputes that such a bundle exists.
stimulation.quote: Using this technique, we found that stimulation of the right inferior parietal lobule or the caudal superior temporal gyrus, but not of its rostral portion, determined rightward deviations on line bisection. However, the strongest shifts occurred with subcortical stimulation. Fiber tracking identified the stimulated site as a section of the superior occipitofrontal fasciculus, a poorly known parietal-frontal pathway.
stimulation.cite: Thiebaut de Schotten M, Urbanski M, Duffau H, et al. Direct evidence for a parietal-frontal pathway subserving spatial awareness in humans. Science. 2005;309(5744):2226-8.

hint: hook-shaped bundle curving around the stem of the sylvian fissure
summary: The uncinate fasciculus is a hook-shaped association bundle that connects the anterior temporal lobe with the orbitofrontal cortex and frontal pole. It curves around the stem of the lateral fissure and passes through the extreme capsule. It is bidirectional and joins memory-related temporal structures with the orbitofrontal regions that assign value. It is part of the ventral limbic system and is linked to social and emotional behaviour. In semantic dementia its integrity is reduced, but cutting it in awake surgery does not reliably cause a language deficit.
where: The model shows the dense core of the bundle from a probabilistic histology atlas. It starts in the anterior temporal lobe near the temporal pole and amygdala, bends sharply upward and forward around the limen insulae, and ends in the orbitofrontal cortex and frontal pole. It lies lateral to the amygdala and medial to the insula. A lateral view with the insula removed or a sagittal view shows the hook.
does: Von Der Heide and colleagues propose that the bundle lets temporal-lobe memory associations, such as a person's name, face and voice, change behaviour through the lateral orbitofrontal cortex, which biases decisions by value. Its bidirectional flow lets reward and punishment history modulate temporal memory representations. It has also been linked to episodic memory, language and social-emotional processing, but its exact function is not well understood. Stimulation data show that its role in language is smaller than that of neighbouring ventral pathways.
connects: It joins the anterior temporal lobe, including the temporal pole and amygdala, with the lateral orbitofrontal cortex and Brodmann area 10. It runs near the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus in the extreme capsule and it is the main white matter link between the two ends of the limbic network in the Yeo parcellation.
clinical: In semantic dementia the uncinate fasciculus shows significantly higher mean diffusivity and lower fractional anisotropy, with loss of word and object knowledge. Abnormalities have been reported in several psychiatric disorders, though findings differ between studies. Surgeons have removed parts of it during awake glioma surgery without a lasting language deficit.
remember: Uncinate means hooked: it hooks from the temporal pole up and forward to the orbitofrontal cortex, linking memory to value.
facts: It connects the anterior temporal lobe with the lateral orbitofrontal cortex and Brodmann area 10.
Subcortical stimulation of it never elicited language disturbances in 13 awake patients.
In semantic dementia it shows higher mean diffusivity and lower fractional anisotropy.

quiz.q: Which hook-shaped bundle joins the anterior temporal lobe with the orbitofrontal cortex?
Semantic dementia shows reduced fractional anisotropy in the arcuate and which bundle linking temporal pole and orbitofrontal cortex?
Which bundle bends around the limen insulae and lies lateral to the amygdala in the extreme capsule region?

how_we_know: Tractography and disease studies show what happens when the bundle is damaged, and awake-surgery stimulation tests language function. Its stimulation result is a negative one: it did not disturb language, which suggests that other ventral pathways can compensate.

evidence.claim: The bundle joins lateral orbitofrontal cortex with the anterior temporal lobe
evidence.finding: Von Der Heide and colleagues reviewed what is known about the uncinate fasciculus. They describe a bidirectional long-range tract linking lateral orbitofrontal cortex and Brodmann area 10 with the anterior temporal lobes, and propose that it lets memory-based associations guide decisions. This is a review of anatomy and clinical findings.
evidence.quote: The uncinate fasciculus is a bidirectional, long-range white matter tract that connects lateral orbitofrontal cortex and Brodmann area 10 with the anterior temporal lobes.
evidence.cite: Von Der Heide RJ, Skipper LM, Klobusicky E, Olson IR. Dissecting the uncinate fasciculus: disorders, controversies and a hypothesis. Brain. 2013;136(Pt 6):1692-707.

evidence.claim: In semantic dementia the uncinate and arcuate fasciculi show lower fractional anisotropy
evidence.finding: Agosta and colleagues tracked language-related pathways with diffusion tensor imaging in five patients with semantic dementia and eight healthy controls. The uncinate and arcuate fasciculi had higher mean diffusivity and lower fractional anisotropy in the patients. This is correlational evidence in a small sample.
evidence.quote: The left inferior longitudinal fasciculus, arcuate fasciculus and fronto-parietal superior longitudinal fasciculus were tracked in five semantic dementia patients and eight healthy controls. The arcuate and uncinate fasciculi demonstrated significantly higher mean diffusivity, parallel and transverse and significantly lower fractional anisotropy.
evidence.cite: Agosta F, Henry RG, Migliaccio R, et al. Language networks in semantic dementia. Brain. 2010;133(Pt 1):286-99.

evidence.claim: Stimulating the left uncinate fasciculus did not disturb language in awake surgery
evidence.finding: Duffau and colleagues studied 13 patients operated awake for a left anterior temporal or orbitofrontal glioma. Stimulating other pathways caused errors, but subcortical stimulation of the uncinate fasciculus never elicited language disturbances. All patients recovered after a transient deficit even though part of the bundle was removed. This is causal evidence that the bundle is not systematically essential for language.
evidence.quote: Interestingly, subcortical stimulation never elicited any language disturbances when performed at the level of the UF. Moreover, after a transient postoperative language deficit, all patients recovered, despite the removal of at least one part of the UF, as confirmed by control MRI.
evidence.cite: Duffau H, Gatignol P, Moritz-Gasser S, Mandonnet E. Is the left uncinate fasciculus essential for language? A cerebral stimulation study. J Neurol. 2009;256(3):382-9.

stimulation.method: direct subcortical electrical stimulation during awake surgery
stimulation.effect: Stimulating the left uncinate fasciculus did not cause any language disturbance in 13 patients, whereas stimulating neighbouring pathways did. All patients recovered after surgery.
stimulation.quote: Interestingly, subcortical stimulation never elicited any language disturbances when performed at the level of the UF. Moreover, after a transient postoperative language deficit, all patients recovered, despite the removal of at least one part of the UF, as confirmed by control MRI.
stimulation.cite: Duffau H, Gatignol P, Moritz-Gasser S, Mandonnet E. Is the left uncinate fasciculus essential for language? A cerebral stimulation study. J Neurol. 2009;256(3):382-9.

hint: C-shaped arch from the hippocampus to the mammillary bodies
summary: The fornix is a C-shaped bundle of axons that carries output from the hippocampal formation to the septal area, hypothalamus and mammillary bodies. It starts as the fimbria along the hippocampus, continues as the crus under the splenium of the corpus callosum, joins its partner as the body, and then splits into columns that arch in front of the interventricular foramen. It is an association and projection pathway in the Papez circuit. The mammillary bodies relay the signal to the anterior thalamic nucleus. Damage to it can cause anterograde amnesia.
where: On a medial view the fornix runs as an arch beneath the corpus callosum, forming the lower margin of the septum pellucidum and the roof of the third ventricle. The model shows the dense core of the bundle from a probabilistic histology atlas, so the fimbria and the finer fibres are underrepresented. The columns descend toward the mammillary bodies in front of the thalamus.
does: It is the main pathway by which the hippocampus communicates with the diencephalon and the septum. Tsivilis and colleagues studied 38 people with surgically removed colloid cysts and found that the volume of the mammillary bodies, which shrink after fornix damage, correlated with 13 of 14 tests of episodic recall but correlated poorly with recognition memory. This fits a view in which recall depends on hippocampal input to the diencephalon. The fornix is not the only route out of the hippocampus, which also projects through the entorhinal cortex.
connects: Fibres arise from the hippocampus and subiculum, run through the fimbria and fornix, and end in the mammillary bodies, the septal nuclei and the anterior thalamus. The mammillary bodies project through the mammillothalamic tract to the anterior thalamic nucleus, which projects to the cingulate cortex in the Papez circuit.
clinical: A penetrating head injury that cut both fornices produced persistent anterograde amnesia in a reported patient without damage to other known memory structures. Colloid cysts of the third ventricle can compress the fornices and cause memory loss. Deep brain stimulation aimed at the fornix has been tested in Alzheimer's disease, with safe surgery but no overall cognitive benefit in a randomised trial of 42 patients.
remember: Fornix means arch: it is the memory arch from hippocampus to mammillary body, which is the first step of the Papez circuit.
facts: It carries hippocampal output to the mammillary bodies, septal nuclei and anterior thalamus.
Mammillary body volume correlated with 13 of 14 episodic recall tests in people with colloid cysts.
Fornix deep brain stimulation in 42 patients with mild Alzheimer's disease showed no overall cognitive benefit.

quiz.q: Which C-shaped bundle carries output from the hippocampus to the mammillary bodies in the Papez circuit?
A penetrating head injury cuts both of these arching fibres and leaves persistent anterograde amnesia. Which structure?
Which arch runs beneath the corpus callosum and ends in columns in front of the thalamus?

how_we_know: Lesions and surgical cases give causal evidence that the fornix matters for recall, and MRI volume studies of people with colloid cysts relate it to memory scores. Deep brain stimulation trials in Alzheimer's disease test whether driving the pathway changes memory circuits, with early signals in a phase I trial and no overall benefit in a randomised phase II trial.

evidence.claim: Isolated damage to both fornices can cause amnesia
evidence.finding: D'Esposito and colleagues reported a patient with a penetrating head injury who developed significant, persistent anterograde amnesia. CT showed a lesion of the posterior parts of both fornices with no evidence of damage to the hippocampus, thalamus or basal forebrain. This is causal evidence in one patient.
evidence.quote: CT revealed a lesion that involved the region of the proximal, posterior portion of both fornices without evidence of damage to other hippocampal pathways or to other structures known to be critical for memory, such as the hippocampus, thalamus, or basal forebrain.
evidence.cite: D'Esposito M, Verfaellie M, Alexander MP, Katz DI. Amnesia following traumatic bilateral fornix transection. Neurology. 1995;45(8):1546-50.

evidence.claim: Fornix and mammillary body volume track recall more than recognition memory
evidence.finding: Tsivilis and colleagues measured 13 brain structures on MRI in 38 people with surgically removed colloid cysts. Mammillary body volume, which indexes fornix damage, correlated with 13 of 14 tests of episodic recall but correlated poorly with recognition memory. No other structure was consistently associated with memory.
evidence.quote: Mammillary body volume significantly correlated with 13 out of 14 tests of episodic memory recall, but correlated poorly with recognition memory.
evidence.cite: Tsivilis D, Vann SD, Denby C, et al. A disproportionate role for the fornix and mammillary bodies in recall versus recognition memory. Nat Neurosci. 2008;11(7):834-42.

data.title: Recall tests correlated with mammillary volume

evidence.claim: In a phase I trial, fornix stimulation activated the memory circuit and the default mode network
evidence.finding: Laxton and colleagues implanted six patients with mild Alzheimer's disease and stimulated continuously for 12 months. Stimulation drove activity in entorhinal and hippocampal areas and in the default mode network, and PET showed a reversal of impaired glucose use in the temporal and parietal lobes. Cognitive results were suggestive in some patients, with no serious adverse events.
evidence.quote: We conducted a phase I trial in 6 patients with mild AD receiving ongoing medication treatment. Patients received continuous stimulation for 12 months. DBS drove neural activity in the memory circuit, including the entorhinal, and hippocampal areas and activated the brain's default mode network.
evidence.cite: Laxton AW, Tang-Wai DF, McAndrews MP, et al. A phase I trial of deep brain stimulation of memory circuits in Alzheimer's disease. Ann Neurol. 2010;68(4):521-34.

evidence.claim: A randomised trial of fornix stimulation in 42 patients found no overall cognitive benefit
evidence.finding: Lozano and colleagues randomised 42 patients with mild Alzheimer's disease to active or sham bilateral stimulation aimed at the fornix. Surgery and stimulation were safe, but there was no significant difference in the primary cognitive outcomes at 12 months. Post-hoc analysis suggested possible benefit in patients aged 65 and older.
evidence.quote: We evaluated active "on" versus sham "off" bilateral DBS directed at the fornix-a major fiber bundle in the brain's memory circuit-in a randomized, double-blind trial (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01608061) in 42 patients with mild AD. There were no significant differences in the primary cognitive outcomes (ADAS-Cog 13, CDR-SB) in the "on" versus "off" stimulation group at 12 months for the whole cohort.
evidence.cite: Lozano AM, Fosdick L, Chakravarty MM, et al. A Phase II Study of Fornix Deep Brain Stimulation in Mild Alzheimer's Disease. J Alzheimers Dis. 2016;54(2):777-87.

stimulation.method: deep brain stimulation of the fornix and hypothalamus
stimulation.effect: Continuous stimulation drove activity in the entorhinal and hippocampal regions and in the default mode network, and temporarily reversed low glucose use in the temporal and parietal lobes. Cognitive changes were possible but not firm in six patients.
stimulation.quote: We conducted a phase I trial in 6 patients with mild AD receiving ongoing medication treatment. Patients received continuous stimulation for 12 months. DBS drove neural activity in the memory circuit, including the entorhinal, and hippocampal areas and activated the brain's default mode network.
stimulation.cite: Laxton AW, Tang-Wai DF, McAndrews MP, et al. A phase I trial of deep brain stimulation of memory circuits in Alzheimer's disease. Ann Neurol. 2010;68(4):521-34.
